title: Get User Input
jobContext: Every login form, every signup page, every search bar — they all start the same way: reading what the user typed.

lesson.content: What's an Input Field?

An <input> is a box on a webpage where users type things. You've used them a million times — the email box on a login page, the search bar on Google. In code, an input looks like this: <input id="email">. That id is how we find it with JavaScript.

<!-- This creates a text box where someone can type their email -->
<input id="email" value="a@b.com">

<!-- The id="email" is like a name tag so JavaScript can find it -->
<!-- The value="a@b.com" is what's currently typed in the box -->
The .value Property

Every input has a .value property. Think of it like a sticky note on the input that says "this is what the user typed right now." If someone types "hello@email.com" into the box, then input.value is "hello@email.com".
document.getElementById('email') finds the input with id="email". The .value part grabs the text inside it. Two steps: find it, then read it.
What's an Object?

An object is a way to group related things together. Like a file folder labeled "User Info" that contains an email and a password inside. In code, we write objects with curly braces { } and use this format: { key: value }.
Your Mission

Write a function called getFormData that finds the email input (id="email") and the password input (id="password"), reads both values, and returns them as an object like { email: "...", password: "..." }. The sandbox already has the inputs set up with values in them.

hints: Same steps for password, then return { email: emailInput.value, password: passwordInput.value }

title: Validate Input
jobContext: Form validation is the most common coding interview question. Companies want to know you can handle bad input — empty fields, wrong formats, short passwords. It's what prevents bugs in production.

lesson.content: Why Validate?

Users make mistakes. They press Submit with empty fields, type 'abc' where an email goes, or use a 3-character password. Validation is checking the data before accepting it. If something's wrong, you tell the user what to fix.
Cleaning Input with .trim()

Users sometimes accidentally add spaces. .trim() is a method that removes spaces from the start and end of text. Think of it like trimming the fat off a piece of meat — you keep the good stuff and remove the excess.
Checking Content with .includes()
An email MUST contain an '@' symbol. .includes('@') checks if '@' is somewhere in the text. It returns true (yes, it's there) or false (no, it's not). This is how we check email format.
Measuring with .length
.length tells you how many characters are in a string. 'hi'.length is 2. 'hello'.length is 5. We use it to enforce password minimums — if the password has fewer than 6 characters, reject it.

let word = 'hello'
console.log(word.length)  // → 5

let password = 'abc'
console.log(password.length)  // → 3

if (password.length < 6) {
  return 'Password must be at least 6 characters'
}
if/else: Making Decisions

if/else is how your code makes decisions. Think: "IF the email is empty, show an error. OTHERWISE, continue checking." You can chain multiple checks — as soon as one fails, the function stops and returns the error message.
Your Mission

Write a function validateLogin(email, password) that runs four checks in order. If a check fails, return the exact error message shown. If all checks pass, return 'valid'. The checks are: (1) empty email → 'Email is required', (2) empty password → 'Password is required', (3) missing @ → 'Invalid email format', (4) password shorter than 6 → 'Password must be at least 6 characters'. Order matters — check them top to bottom!

testCases.name: rejects short password
testCases.expected: Password must be at least 6 characters

hints: Use .trim() before checking if something is empty — spaces count as characters!
.includes('@') returns true if the text contains @, false otherwise
.length gives you the character count — 'hi'.length is 2
Check conditions in order: email empty → password empty → invalid email → short password
As soon as you hit a problem, return the error message and stop

title: Submit & Handle
jobContext: Every form on the web — signups, checkouts, search bars — uses this exact pattern. Without preventDefault(), the page refreshes and you lose everything.

lesson.content: How Forms Normally Work

When you click a Submit button on a webpage, the browser's default behavior is to reload the page and send the data somewhere. That's fine for old-school websites, but bad for modern apps — it wipes everything and feels jarring. We need to intercept the submit and handle it ourselves.
addEventListener: Listening for Actions

addEventListener is like telling JavaScript "keep an eye on this element, and when THIS thing happens, run THIS code." The first argument is the event type ('submit' for forms, 'click' for buttons). The second argument is a function that runs when the event happens.
e.preventDefault(): The Page-Reload Stopper

The 'e' in addEventListener('submit', function(e) { ... }) is short for 'event object.' It's a special object that contains information about what happened. One of its methods is .preventDefault(), which stops the browser from doing its default behavior — in this case, reloading the page.
Putting It All Together

Here's the full pattern: Find the form. Listen for submit. Stop the reload. Read the inputs. Check if the data is valid. Show a result on the page. Every form handler in the world follows these steps in order.
Your Mission

Write a function handleSubmit() that does THREE things: (1) finds the form with id='login-form', (2) attaches a submit listener that calls e.preventDefault(), and (3) reads login-email and login-password and shows the combined result in the div with id='result'. The sandbox already has the HTML set up.

hints: document.getElementById('login-form') finds the form by its id
Use .addEventListener('submit', function(e) { ... }) to listen for submits
e.preventDefault() is the FIRST thing inside your submit handler — before any other code
document.getElementById('login-email').value reads what's in an input in one line
result.textContent = '...' shows text inside the result div
